analysis.one_liner: Extends federal child labor protections to independent contractors and sharply increases penalties for violations.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate committee that received it; it died without a vote or hearing in the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would close a loophole in the federal Fair Labor Standards Act: today, child labor rules only cover formal employees, so a business can engage a 15-year-old as an 'independent contractor' and fall outside the rules. The bill rewrites the law so anyone who engages a minor for paid work is covered, and raises the penalties for violations — from a maximum of $11,000 per violation to fines of up to $132,270, and up to $601,150 when a violation causes serious injury or death, with the amounts rising each year with inflation. Repeat or willful violators could face a $50,000 fine and up to a year in prison.
analysis.who_benefits: Working minors — especially teenagers in hazardous industries like meatpacking, agriculture, and staffing-firm placements, where independent-contractor arrangements and subcontracting have been used to evade child labor rules. The bill gives the Labor Department real leverage: minimum $5,000 fines, much higher maximums, and criminal penalties for repeat or willful violators.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Minors working for pay, especially in hazardous jobs

how_it_helps.text: The bill expands the definition of 'employer' under the Fair Labor Standards Act so that, for child labor purposes, it includes 'any person engaging an individual (including an independent contractor) for the performance of work,' closing the contractor loophole. [S2] [S3]

It replaces the current maximum civil penalty of $11,000 per violation with a range of $5,000 to $132,270, and $25,000 to $601,150 for violations causing death or serious injury, with amounts adjusted annually for inflation. [S2] [S3]
Repeat or willful violators of child labor provisions would face criminal fines up to $50,000 and up to one year of imprisonment. [S2] [S3]
The bill also expands the definition of 'work' to include 'the performance of services for remuneration,' so the protections follow the money rather than the employment label. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that use minor workers through subcontractor, staffing, or gig-style arrangements — staffing firms, agricultural employers, meatpackers and their labor contractors — would face the new higher fines and exposure to criminal charges. Businesses that already comply would pay nothing.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers using minors through contractor arrangements

drawbacks.text: Raising minimum penalties to $5,000 per violation could impose significant costs on small, family-run businesses — farms and small shops that employ teens in summer jobs — where paperwork mistakes are more common than willful exploitation. [S2] [S3]

Extending 'employer' status to anyone engaging an independent contractor for work could create legal uncertainty for gig-style platforms and legitimate small contractors who hire teens for errands or side work, since the bill does not create a separate carve-out for benign arrangements. [S3]

A good-faith objection is that criminal liability for 'repeat' violations could reach business owners whose subcontractors hired minors without their knowledge, since the bill holds anyone engaging a worker liable under the child labor provisions. [S2] [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core fix is well targeted: child labor law written in 1938 assumed formal employment, and the bill updates it so contractor arrangements cannot be used to avoid it. The steep new penalties are the main cost risk — the $5,000 minimum could fall hard on small operations that make paperwork mistakes rather than exploit children. A narrower bill might have scaled penalties by business size, but the protections themselves address a real enforcement gap.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate's labor committee, which never acted on it — no hearing, no vote — and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Schatz introduced the bill on March 2, 2023, with five original cosponsors: Fetterman, Durbin, Cortez Masto, Baldwin, and Duckworth. [S3]
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions. [S5]
Twelve Senate Democrats total cosponsored the bill, all Democrats; no Republican cosponsor signed on. [S4]
The action history shows no further action after the committee referral — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — for the rest of the Congress, which ended January 3, 2025. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that engage minors through independent-contractor or subcontracting arrangements are better off, because the loophole they operate through stays open and penalty levels stay at the old $11,000 maximum. Teenagers in hazardous industries remain exposed to the same risks the bill targeted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers using contractor loopholes; compliant small businesses unchanged

against.what_they_did: None of the 49 Senate Republicans cosponsored the bill, leaving it without cross-party support that its committee fate would have required.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats — 12 of the Senate's 48 Democrats plus independent-caucus Sen. Schatz — and no Republican signed on; the bill died in committee without any roll call to test wider support.

industries.note: These firms place workers — including minors — through contractor and subcontractor arrangements that sit outside current child labor rules. The bill would make anyone engaging a minor for paid work an 'employer' under child labor law, exposing them to fines up to $132,270 per violation. [S2] [S3]

The industry and its cleaning and labor contractors have relied on subcontracted, sometimes underage, workers, and contractor status is part of how that labor is arranged. Higher penalties — up to $601,150 for violations causing serious injury or death — would raise the cost of those arrangements. [S2] [S3]

industries.industry: Agriculture and small employers of teens
industries.note: Farms and small businesses that legitimately employ teens would face the new $5,000 minimum penalty for paperwork violations, a real compliance cost, though the tightened contractor rules mainly threaten arrangements used to dodge the rules. [S2] [S3]
